clips.text: [cultivated British voice, museum documentary, grave and completely sincere] An opening, it turns out, is made almost entirely of whatever surrounds it. We have spent the past eighteen months surrounding one... very carefully, and at considerable expense. [quiet emphasis] This is the shape of openness.

[cultivated British voice, reverent, measured] Our research began in the caves of southern France, some thirty thousand years before the alphabet. Someone pressed a hand against the rock... and blew red ochre around it. When the hand was taken away, it left behind the first logo made entirely of what isn't there. [dry, solemn] All of this was achieved without a brand guidelines PDF, which our studio still finds very difficult to discuss.

[cultivated British voice, precise, quietly awestruck] Euclid defined the circle as every point at the same distance from a centre: a promise kept all the way round, without a single corner to hide behind. We admired it enormously. [deliberate emphasis] And then, with genuine regret, we left it out. The mark contains no curves whatsoever.

[cultivated British voice, professorial seriousness] Draw a second circle through the centre of the first, and the overlap is called the vesica piscis: Latin for the bladder of a fish, and generally left in Latin. [restrained] Gothic masons drew their pointed arches from it. We had one framed, and hung it above the rectangle, in the hope that something might rub off.

[cultivated British voice, exacting, deadpan] No identity can be taken seriously without consulting the golden ratio, so we measured ours with tremendous ceremony. The mark is exactly one and a quarter times taller than it is wide. The golden ratio is one point six one eight. [unhurried, final] It was thanked for its time, and shown out through a side door.

[cultivated British voice, intimate scholarly authority] According to Vasari, when the Pope sent for proof of Giotto's talent, Giotto dipped a brush in red, drew a perfect circle freehand, and sent nothing else. [serious] When we were asked for something similar, we sent four right angles and a hundred and twelve page rationale. [deadpan] We are still waiting to hear back.

[cultivated British voice, dark documentary gravity] Dante arranged Hell as nine circles, each narrower than the last, descending towards a centre that is not on fire, as is commonly assumed, but frozen solid. [quiet, devastating seriousness] We went all the way down, purely for research, and came back with some very firm views on onboarding.

[cultivated British voice, crisp and authoritative] Beneath everything lies a grid, four modules wide and five high, each module sixty units square. Fourteen of the twenty become wall. The remaining six stay inside, where they do the vital work of not being wall. [reverent] It is the most carefully arranged nothing we have ever been paid for.

[cultivated British voice, forensic calm] Typographers call the space inside a letter its counter. Ours has a floor, a quieter grey plane across the lower two thirds, so that nobody falls through. [measured] By area, the mark is seventy per cent wall, twenty per cent floor, and ten per cent clear air, [soft, utterly earnest] which now has its own chapter in the brand guidelines.

[cultivated British voice, precise, measured] Shapes that measure the same rarely look the same, so the walls were thickened until they looked right, and then thinned until they looked deliberate. [dry] The wordmark received similar care. Spaced too generously, its letters seem to be leaving one another. Too tightly, and someone from Legal starts using the word merger.

[cultivated British voice, prestigious design documentary, sincere] One early proposal set the thermal energy of red against the contemplative depth of blue, held apart by a gentle white smile. Focus groups recognised it instantly, which was encouraging, until we asked what they thought they had recognised. [cold, administrative finality] The proposal was rejected. Its designer now works in soft drinks.

[cultivated British voice, brisk museum curator] Other studies followed. Two overlapping circles felt too much like a credit card, and a target felt faintly threatening. A red oval turned out to be a web browser, a rounded square kept asking to be an app icon, and the golden rectangle tried to get back in through the side door. [slow, solemn] Each taught us something about what the mark must never become.

[cultivated British voice, quietly transcendent, entirely sincere] And so, after the caves, the compass, nine circles of Hell, and a colleague's sudden move into soft drinks, we arrived back where we began: a rectangle, with a hole in it. [long pause, intimate conviction] It may be the most important hole of our careers. [warm, final] OpenCode. Do come in.
